### The Structure of Bayesian Stable Matchings with Transfers

Classical matching theory gives stable outcomes a distinct structure: an identical set of unmatched agents across stable outcomes (the Lone Wolf theorem). Hu (2026) shows that under incomplete information matching without transfers, the Lone Wolf property survives whenever stable outcomes share a common information structure. I show that this is almost false under incomplete information matching with transfers, and give a necessary and sufficient condition under which the Lone Wolf theorem holds generically.

### Search and Matching with Bilateral Information Acquisition

We study a search-and-matching market in which agents can costly acquire information about a potential partner before deciding whether to match. Higher-type agents are both more selective and acquire more precise information, generating assortative information acquisition. We establish equilibrium existence and show that, despite the endogenous acceptance curse, equilibrium matching exhibits stochastic positive assortative sorting.

### A Noncooperative Foundation for Bayesian Stable Matching

We study a decentralized matching market with transfers and privately informed workers, where randomly drawn wage offers are publicly tendered and accepted or rejected, and employers learn the types of workers they hire. When agents are sufficiently impatient relative to small adjustment costs, the game has an essentially unique equilibrium, play converges almost surely in finite time, and every terminal state is Bayesian stable in the sense of Liu (2020) and Chen and Hu (2024).

### Deliberation by Ballot: Communication and Consensus in Elections by Repeated Voting

Some of the oldest consensus institutions — conclaves, juries, conventions — do not separate deliberation from voting: members communicate by voting, casting repeated ballots until a supermajority forms. I model committees in which each ballot is semi-binding communication about private information and private biases.
